name: Data Structures
author: Recurse
subject: cs
description: How lists, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash maps, trees, heaps and graphs store data, and when to use each.

lesson.intro: A data structure is a way of organizing data so that the operations you need are fast. The same data stored in a list, a dict or a heap behaves very differently, so picking the right one often matters more than clever code.

sections.title: Arrays and linked lists
sections.body:
A Python list is a dynamic array: its items sit side by side in one block of memory, so the computer can jump straight to any index. Reading or writing `nums[i]` is O(1), and `append` at the end is O(1) amortized.

The price is paid at the front and in the middle. `nums.insert(0, x)` must shift every existing item one slot to the right, which is O(n). `nums.pop(0)` shifts everything left, also O(n).

A linked list stores each item in its own node, and each node holds a reference to the next one. Adding or removing a node next to one you already hold only changes a couple of references: O(1). But there is no way to jump to position i. You must follow `next` links from the head, which is O(n).

- Fast access by index: array (Python list).
- Many inserts and removals at a position you already hold: linked list.
sections.code:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
print(nums[1])         # 20: jumps straight to slot 1
nums.insert(0, 5)      # every existing item shifts right
print(nums)            # [5, 10, 20, 30]

class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next=None):
        self.value = value
        self.next = next

head = Node(10, Node(20, Node(30)))
head = Node(5, head)   # new front node: nothing shifts
node = head
while node:            # reaching item i means walking i links
    print(node.value)
    node = node.next
sections.tip: In everyday Python you rarely write a linked list yourself; collections.deque covers most cases where you would want one.

check.question: You read items by position millions of times and almost never insert. Which structure fits best?
choices: A linked list, because nodes are easy to add
A deque, because it is fast at both ends
A Python list, because indexing is O(1)
Either list type: both reach index i in one step
check.explanation: A list computes the address of slot i directly. A linked list must follow i links from the head, which is O(n). Fast insertion is the linked list's strength, but this workload does not need it.

sections.title: Stacks and queues
sections.body:
A stack is last in, first out (LIFO): you add and remove at the same end, like a pile of plates. Undo history, the Back button and the function call stack all work this way. A Python list makes a good stack: `append` pushes and `pop()` removes the last item, both O(1).

A queue is first in, first out (FIFO): items leave in the order they arrived, like a line at a shop. Print jobs, task queues and breadth-first search all use queues.

Do not build a queue from a list with `pop(0)`. Each call shifts every remaining item, so it is O(n). Use `collections.deque`, which adds and removes at both ends in O(1): `append` joins the back and `popleft` leaves from the front.
sections.code:
from collections import deque

stack = []
stack.append("a")
stack.append("b")
print(stack.pop())       # b: last in, first out

queue = deque()
queue.append("a")
queue.append("b")
print(queue.popleft())   # a: first in, first out
sections.tip: Ask which item should come out next: the newest (stack) or the oldest (queue).

check.question: Which structure fits a browser's Back button?
choices: A queue
A stack
A set
A heap
check.explanation: Back returns to the most recently visited page first: last in, first out. A queue would send you back to the first page you opened.

sections.title: Hash maps and sets
sections.body:
A hash map stores key-value pairs. A hash function turns each key into a number that picks a slot in an internal table, so finding a key does not require scanning. Python's `dict` is a hash map: lookup, insert and delete are O(1) on average.

Two different keys can land in the same slot. This is a collision: the table keeps both and compares the actual keys when looking one up. Collisions are why the worst case is O(n), but a good hash function and automatic resizing keep that rare.

Keys must be hashable, meaning their hash can never change. Immutable values such as `str`, `int` and tuples of them work. A `list` does not, because it could change after being stored.

A `set` is a hash map with keys and no values. Use it to remove duplicates or test membership: `x in my_set` is O(1) on average, while `x in my_list` checks items one by one, O(n).
sections.code:
ages = {"ana": 31, "ben": 25}
ages["cy"] = 40              # insert: O(1) on average
print(ages.get("dee", 0))    # 0: missing key gives the default

seen = set()
for word in ["to", "be", "or", "not", "to", "be"]:
    if word in seen:         # membership: O(1) on average
        print("repeat:", word)
    seen.add(word)
sections.tip: Dicts remember insertion order (Python 3.7 and later); sets have no guaranteed order.

check.question: Why does `d[[1, 2]] = "x"` raise a TypeError?
choices: Dict keys must be strings
The list has more than one item
Dicts cannot store string values
Lists are mutable, so they are not hashable
check.explanation: A key's hash must never change, or the dict could not find it again. Lists can change, so Python refuses them as keys; the tuple (1, 2) works. Keys do not have to be strings: ints and tuples are fine.

sections.title: Trees, BSTs and heaps
sections.body:
A tree is a set of nodes with one root, where each node can have children and there are no cycles. In a binary tree each node has at most two children, `left` and `right`.

A binary search tree (BST) adds a rule: every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node, and every key in its right subtree is larger. A search compares with the current node and goes left or right, discarding a whole subtree each step. In a balanced tree that is O(log n). Insert keys in sorted order into a plain BST, though, and every node goes right: the tree becomes a chain and search is O(n). Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) prevent this. An in-order traversal (left, node, right) visits the keys in sorted order.

A heap is a different kind of tree. In a min-heap every parent is less than or equal to its children, so the smallest item is always at the root. Peeking at it is O(1); adding an item or removing the smallest is O(log n). A heap is not fully sorted: only parent-child pairs are ordered. Python's `heapq` keeps a min-heap inside a plain list, and heaps power priority queues.
sections.tip: For a max-heap with heapq, push negated numbers and negate them again when you pop.

check.question: You insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, in that order, into a plain BST with no balancing. What is searching for 5 like?
choices: It walks a chain of 5 nodes: O(n)
It takes about log2(5) steps: O(log n)
It takes one step, because 5 is the root
It fails, because a BST rejects sorted input
check.explanation: Each new key is larger than every key before it, so it always goes right. The tree turns into a linked list and search is O(n). The root is 1, the first key inserted. Balanced trees avoid this by rotating nodes to keep the height near log n.

sections.title: Graphs and choosing a structure
sections.body:
A graph is a set of vertices (nodes) joined by edges. Edges can be directed (one-way, like following someone) or undirected (two-way, like a friendship), and can carry weights such as distances.

An adjacency list maps each vertex to a list of its neighbors. It uses O(V + E) memory, and listing a vertex's neighbors is fast. An adjacency matrix is a V by V grid where cell [i][j] is 1 when there is an edge. It answers "is there an edge from i to j?" in O(1), but always uses O(V^2) memory, and listing neighbors takes O(V). Most real graphs are sparse (each vertex touches only a few others), so the adjacency list is the usual default.

To choose any structure, start from the operation you do most:

- Access by position, keep order: list.
- Add or remove at both ends: deque.
- Look up by key, or test membership: dict or set.
- Repeatedly take the smallest or largest item: heap.
- Keep items sorted with fast search and insert: balanced BST.
- Model connections between things: graph.
sections.code:
# Undirected graph with edges A-B, A-C, B-D
adj_list = {
    "A": ["B", "C"],
    "B": ["A", "D"],
    "C": ["A"],
    "D": ["B"],
}

#             A  B  C  D
adj_matrix = [[0, 1, 1, 0],   # A
              [1, 0, 0, 1],   # B
              [1, 0, 0, 0],   # C
              [0, 1, 0, 0]]   # D

print(adj_list["B"])          # ['A', 'D']: neighbors of B
print(adj_matrix[0][3] == 1)  # False: no edge between A and D

check.question: A social network has 1 million users with about 200 friends each. How should you store the friendships?
choices: As an adjacency matrix, since edge checks are O(1)
As an adjacency list, since the graph is sparse
As a heap keyed by user id
As one sorted list of all users
check.explanation: A matrix would need 10^12 cells, almost all of them 0. An adjacency list stores about 200 million entries (each friendship appears in two lists), which is far smaller. O(1) edge checks do not justify a trillion cells.

keyTerms.definition: A list stored in one contiguous block with spare capacity; indexing is O(1) and appending is O(1) amortized.
A chain of nodes where each node holds a value and a reference to the next node.
A last in, first out (LIFO) collection: items are added and removed at the same end.
A first in, first out (FIFO) collection: items leave in the order they arrived.
A key-value store that uses a hash of each key to find its slot, giving O(1) average lookup.
A binary tree where keys in a node's left subtree are smaller and keys in its right subtree are larger.
A tree where every parent is ordered before its children, so the minimum (or maximum) sits at the root.
A graph representation that maps each vertex to a list of its neighbors.

summary: Lists give O(1) indexing but O(n) inserts at the front; linked lists flip that trade-off.
Use a list as a stack and collections.deque as a queue; list.pop(0) is O(n).
Dicts and sets give O(1) average lookup by key, and keys must be hashable.
A balanced BST keeps search O(log n); a heap gives the smallest item in O(1) and removes it in O(log n).
Store most graphs as adjacency lists, and choose any structure by the operation you do most.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who has never programmed why finding a word in a dict is fast but finding it in a list can be slow, and describe one situation where you would still choose a list.

questions.question: Which operation on a Python list of n items is O(n)?
choices: nums[500]
nums.append(x)
nums.insert(0, x)
len(nums)
questions.explanation: Inserting at index 0 shifts every existing item one slot right, so the work grows with n. Indexing and len are O(1), and append writes into spare capacity at the end, which is O(1) amortized.

questions.question: You already hold a reference to a node in the middle of a singly linked list. What does it cost to insert a new node right after it?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Only two references change: the new node points to the old next node, and the current node points to the new one. The O(n) cost people expect is for finding the position by walking from the head, which has already been done here.

questions.question: This function should return the number of nodes in a linked list. What is wrong?
questions.code:
def length(head):
    count = 0
    node = head
    while node.next:
        count += 1
        node = node.next
    return count
choices: count should start at 1 instead of 0
The loop tests node.next instead of node, so it skips the last node and crashes on an empty list
node = node.next should come before count += 1
A linked list cannot be walked with a while loop
questions.explanation: With `while node.next`, the loop stops while standing on the last node without counting it, so a 3-node list returns 2. On an empty list head is None, and None.next raises AttributeError. `while node:` fixes both. Starting count at 1 fixes non-empty lists but still crashes on an empty one.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.code:
stack = []
for x in [1, 2, 3]:
    stack.append(x)
stack.pop()
stack.append(4)
print(stack.pop() + stack.pop())
questions.explanation: After pushing 1, 2 and 3 the stack is [1, 2, 3]. pop() removes 3, then 4 is pushed: [1, 2, 4]. The next two pops return 4 and then 2, so it prints 6. A queue would have removed 1 first.

questions.question: Fill the blank to remove and return the item that joined the queue first.
questions.code:
from collections import deque

queue = deque(["a", "b", "c"])
first = queue._____()
print(first)  # a
choices: pop
shift
dequeue
popleft
questions.explanation: popleft removes from the front of a deque in O(1), giving first in, first out order. pop removes from the right end and would return 'c'. shift and dequeue are names from other languages; deque has neither method.

questions.question: This bracket checker returns False for "([])", which is balanced. What is the bug?
choices: ch in "([" should be ch in pairs
It should return True instead of not stack
stack.pop(0) takes the oldest opener; stack.pop() would take the most recent one
The pairs dict maps closers to openers backwards
questions.explanation: Brackets close in the reverse order they opened, which is exactly last in, first out. When ']' arrives, its partner is the newest opener, '['. pop(0) takes '(' from the bottom instead. Returning `not stack` is correct: it rejects text that leaves an opener unclosed.

questions.question: Your program receives 100,000 IDs and must report each one it has seen before. Which type should seen be?
choices: list
set
tuple
deque
questions.explanation: `id in seen` is O(1) on average for a set, so the whole job is about O(n). For a list or a deque each check scans the items, making the job O(n^2). A tuple cannot even be added to.

questions.question: What is the average time complexity of `key in d` for a Python dict with n keys? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: The key's hash points straight to the slot where it would be, so the cost does not grow with n. It only becomes O(n) in the rare worst case where many keys collide.

questions.question: This should count how often each word appears. What goes wrong?
choices: counts[word] += 1 raises KeyError the first time a word is seen
Dict keys cannot be strings
It prints {'red': 1, 'blue': 1} because dicts ignore repeats
counts must be created with dict() instead of {}
questions.explanation: `+=` reads counts[word] before writing it, and reading a missing key raises KeyError. Use `counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1` or collections.Counter. {} and dict() create the same empty dict.

questions.question: Two different keys hash to the same slot in a hash map. What happens?
choices: The second key silently replaces the first
Python raises a KeyError on insert
The map is rebuilt so that no collisions can happen again
Both are stored, and lookups compare keys to find the right one
questions.explanation: Collisions are normal. The table keeps both entries, by probing for another slot or chaining, and compares the actual keys during lookup. Only an equal key replaces a value; a different key with the same hash never overwrites it.

questions.question: You insert 8, 3, 10, 1, 6 into an empty BST, in that order. What does an in-order traversal return?
questions.explanation: In-order visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree, which in a BST always yields the keys in sorted order. [8, 3, 1, 6, 10] is the pre-order (node first) and [1, 6, 3, 10, 8] is the post-order (node last).

questions.question: Fill the blank so this BST search goes the right way at each node.
questions.explanation: Smaller keys live in the left subtree, so when key < node.key the search must go left. With > the search turns the wrong way at every node and misses keys that are in the tree.

questions.question: A min-heap holds n items. What is the time complexity of heapq.heappop? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: Popping removes the root, moves the last item to the top and sifts it down one level at a time. A heap is a complete binary tree about log2(n) levels deep, so this is O(log n). Only peeking at heap[0] is O(1).

questions.question: After heapq.heapify(nums) on a list of distinct numbers, which statement is always true?
choices: nums is sorted in ascending order
nums[1] is the second smallest item
nums[-1] is the largest item
nums[0] is the smallest item
questions.explanation: A min-heap only promises that each parent is less than or equal to its children, which puts the minimum at index 0. The rest is only partly ordered: the second smallest may be at index 1 or 2, and the list is usually not sorted. heapify([1, 5, 2]) leaves it as [1, 5, 2].

questions.question: A graph has V vertices and E edges. In Big-O, how much memory does an adjacency list need?
questions.explanation: It stores one entry per vertex plus one list item per edge (two for an undirected edge, which is still O(E)). An adjacency matrix needs O(V^2) no matter how few edges there are.

questions.question: A server must always run the waiting job with the highest priority next, while new jobs keep arriving. Which structure fits best?
choices: A queue (deque)
A list sorted again after each insert
A heap
A set
questions.explanation: A heap gives the top-priority item in O(1) and supports insert and remove in O(log n). Keeping a list sorted costs at least O(n) per insert, and a plain queue serves jobs by arrival time, not priority.

questions.question: When would you pick an adjacency matrix instead of an adjacency list?
questions.answer: When the graph is dense (most pairs of vertices are connected) or when you must check whether a specific edge exists very often. The matrix answers that in O(1) but always costs O(V^2) memory.
questions.explanation: For sparse graphs, which most real graphs are, the O(V^2) matrix is mostly zeros, so adjacency lists are the default.
